```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(message = FALSE, warning = FALSE)
```

This document is the R counterpart of the Python notebook
[Part 05 - Time Series and Causal Inference](../../Notebooks/Part%2005%20-%20Time%20Series%20and%20Causal%20Inference/Part%2005%20-%20Time%20Series%20and%20Causal%20Inference.ipynb).
It turns posting histories into time series, describes their rhythms,
and then asks a harder question: did a real-world event *cause* a change
in behavior? The same two quasi-experimental designs — interrupted time
series and difference-in-differences — are fit here with base R's `lm()`
in place of statsmodels.

Both versions analyze **the same saved archive**, so they should agree
exactly. Section 5 checks that they do: R's regression coefficients are
compared with the table the Python notebook saved.

### Learning objectives

* Collect posting histories, decide when to stop, and analyze a saved archive.
* Handle timestamps and timezones.
* Describe diurnal, weekly, and seasonal posting rhythms.
* Fit and interpret an interrupted time series (ITS) regression.
* Fit difference-in-differences (DiD) and check the parallel-trends assumption.
* Articulate the threats to validity that observational designs face.

## Setup

```{r libraries}
library(bskyr)
library(tidyverse)
library(jsonlite)
library(lubridate)
```

As in every part of this series, the shared helper `bsky_client.R` looks
for credentials (an `atproto.json` file or bskyr's environment
variables), authenticates if it finds them, and sets `bsky_authed`. Most
parts gate *every* chunk on that flag, because bskyr needs credentials
for every call. This part is different. The analysis runs on a saved
archive, so it works **without** credentials; only the chunks that call
the API (re-collecting the archive, matching, keyword search) are gated
on `bsky_authed`.

```{r connect}
source("bsky_client.R")
```

## 1. Collecting posting histories, and why we analyze a saved archive

The event we will study is the November 2024 US election and the surge
of Twitter-to-Bluesky migration that followed it. We need two histories
that reach well back before the event: a *treated* account (The New York
Times, a newsroom whose Bluesky audience exploded during the surge) and a
*comparison* account (`bsky.app`, the platform's official account).

**An author feed is returned newest first.** To reach November 2024 we
have to page through *everything* the account has posted since, and a
newsroom keeps posting every day. In mid-2026 a fixed budget of about
40,000 items reached comfortably past the event. By November 2026 the
same budget stopped two months *after* it, the pre-event period silently
disappeared, and every causal estimate failed. A collection designed
around today's data ages, sometimes in months.

So this document separates **collecting** from **analyzing**:

* By default it reads the **archive saved by the Python notebook**,
  `actions.csv.gz`: one row per action, keeping only the account, the
  action type, a reply flag, and the timestamp (data minimization: no
  URIs, no text, no engagement counts). Every number below is then
  reproducible.
* With the environment variable `PART05_REFRESH=1` set and credentials
  available, the `refresh` chunk re-collects the archive with bskyr and
  writes it next to this document instead. That takes about 500
  requests, which is why it is opt-in.

```{r params, eval=TRUE}
TREATED <- "nytimes.com"
COMPARISON <- "bsky.app"
EVENT <- as_date("2024-11-05")
TZ <- "America/New_York"

SHARED_ARCHIVE <- file.path("..", "..", "Notebooks",
                            "Part 05 - Time Series and Causal Inference",
                            "data", "actions.csv.gz")
LOCAL_ARCHIVE <- file.path("data", "actions.csv.gz")

REFRESH <- Sys.getenv("PART05_REFRESH") == "1"
```

The refresh pages through each account's history with
[`bs_get_author_feed()`](https://christophertkenny.com/bskyr/reference/bs_get_author_feed.html), sizing its budget
from the post count in [`bs_get_profile()`](https://christophertkenny.com/bskyr/reference/bs_get_profile.html). It reads
raw API pages (`clean = FALSE`), so it can classify
each feed item directly: an item with a `reason` of type
`#reasonRepost` is a repost, and it is timestamped by *when the account
reposted* (`reason$indexedAt`) rather than when the original post was
written. A reply is a post whose record carries a `reply` field.

```{r refresh, eval = bsky_authed && REFRESH}
budget_items <- function(actor) {
  # One item per post, ~25% extra for reposts, plus slack
  ceiling(bs_get_profile(actor)$posts_count * 1.25) + 2000
}

collect_actions <- function(actor) {
  pages <- bs_get_author_feed(actor, limit = budget_items(actor), clean = FALSE)
  items <- list_flatten(map(pages, "feed"))
  map(items, \(item) {
    is_repost <- identical(item$reason$`$type`, "app.bsky.feed.defs#reasonRepost")
    tibble(
      actor = actor,
      action = if (is_repost) "repost" else "post",
      is_reply = !is.null(item$post$record$reply),
      created_at = if (is_repost) item$reason$indexedAt else item$post$record$createdAt
    )
  }) |> list_rbind()
}

dir.create("data", showWarnings = FALSE)
bind_rows(collect_actions(TREATED), collect_actions(COMPARISON)) |>
  mutate(created_at = format(ymd_hms(created_at, tz = "UTC"), "%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ")) |>
  arrange(actor, created_at) |>
  write_csv(LOCAL_ARCHIVE)
```

```{r load, eval=TRUE}
ARCHIVE <- if (REFRESH && file.exists(LOCAL_ARCHIVE)) LOCAL_ARCHIVE else SHARED_ARCHIVE

archive_metadata <- read_json(file.path(dirname(SHARED_ARCHIVE), "collection_metadata.json"))
archive_metadata$collected_at

read_csv(ARCHIVE, show_col_types = FALSE) |> head()
```

Each row is one action, stored with its timestamp as a UTC string (the
trailing `Z`). The archive reaches back to November 2023 for
`nytimes.com` — a full year before the event — and stops there by
design.

## 2. Timestamps and timezones

API timestamps are UTC; humans live in local time, and diurnal rhythms
only make sense in the timezone where the humans behind the account
work — for a New York newsroom, Eastern time. We parse each timestamp
with `ymd_hms(tz = "UTC")` and convert it with `with_tz()`. We name the
*zone*, not an offset: the zone database knows New York is UTC−4 in
summer and UTC−5 in winter, so daylight-saving transitions are handled
for us.

```{r timestamps, eval=TRUE}
archive <- read_csv(ARCHIVE, show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(created_at = with_tz(ymd_hms(created_at, tz = "UTC"), TZ)) |>
  arrange(created_at)

treated_posts <- filter(archive, actor == TREATED)
comparison_posts <- filter(archive, actor == COMPARISON)

count(treated_posts, action)
sum(treated_posts$is_reply)
```

Original posts dominate: reposts are under a tenth of the newsroom's
activity, and replies are rare. An institutional account broadcasts; it
seldom converses.

## 3. Descriptive time series: the rhythms of posting

### Daily counts and a rolling mean

Counting actions per day gives a noisy series; a *rolling mean* smooths
it so the trend is visible. Two details: `complete()` fills in
zero-count days (a day with no posts is data, not a gap!), and
`stats::filter()` with equal weights of 1/k computes a centered k-day
moving average — base R's one-line rolling mean:

```{r daily, eval=TRUE, fig.width=10, fig.height=4}
daily_counts <- function(posts) {
  posts |>
    count(date = as_date(created_at, tz = TZ)) |>
    complete(date = seq(min(date), max(date), by = "day"),
             fill = list(n = 0))
}

rolling_mean <- function(x, k = 28) {
  as.numeric(stats::filter(x, rep(1 / k, k), sides = 2))
}

treated_daily <- daily_counts(treated_posts)

treated_daily |>
  mutate(rolling = rolling_mean(n)) |>
  ggplot(aes(date)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = n), color = "lightsteelblue", linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_line(aes(y = rolling), color = "navy", linewidth = 1) +
  labs(x = "Date", y = "Actions per day",
       title = paste("Daily activity:", TREATED),
       subtitle = "28-day centered rolling mean in navy") +
  theme_minimal()
```

Activity rises through spring 2024, sags to the lowest level of the
whole series in late summer and fall 2024, and then — in the weeks after
the November election — climbs to roughly four times its old level and
*stays there*. That is a **step**, not a spike: there is no decay back
toward the old baseline.

### Weekly counts

Weeks are the unit of analysis for the causal designs. To match the
Python notebook exactly, a week runs Monday through Sunday and is
labelled by its Sunday. That is what pandas' `resample('W')` does, and
here it is `floor_date(..., week_start = 1) + 6` days. We also drop the
final week, which is usually incomplete because collection happened
partway through it:

```{r weekly, eval=TRUE, fig.width=10, fig.height=4}
weekly_counts <- function(posts) {
  posts |>
    mutate(week = as_date(floor_date(created_at, "week", week_start = 1), tz = TZ) + 6) |>
    count(week) |>
    complete(week = seq(min(week), max(week), by = "week"),
             fill = list(n = 0)) |>
    filter(week != max(week))          # drop the final, incomplete week
}

treated_weekly <- weekly_counts(treated_posts)

ggplot(treated_weekly, aes(week, n)) +
  geom_line(color = "navy") +
  labs(x = "Week", y = "Actions per week",
       title = paste("Weekly activity:", TREATED)) +
  theme_minimal()
```

### Hour-of-day and day-of-week profiles

The same actions binned by local hour and by UTC hour tell two different
stories, and only the local one matches a plausible working day:

```{r rhythms, eval=TRUE, fig.width=10, fig.height=4}
bind_rows(
  count(treated_posts, hour = hour(created_at)) |> mutate(clock = TZ),
  count(treated_posts, hour = hour(with_tz(created_at, "UTC"))) |> mutate(clock = "UTC")
) |>
  ggplot(aes(hour, n, color = clock)) +
  geom_line() + geom_point() +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 22, 2)) +
  labs(x = "Hour of day", y = "Total actions", color = NULL,
       title = paste("Diurnal profile:", TREATED)) +
  theme_minimal()

treated_posts |>
  count(dow = wday(created_at, label = TRUE, week_start = 1)) |>
  ggplot(aes(dow, n)) +
  geom_col(fill = "navy", alpha = 0.85) +
  labs(x = "Day of week", y = "Total actions",
       title = paste("Weekly rhythm:", TREATED)) +
  theme_minimal()
```

In New York time the account is quiet from midnight to about 6 AM and
peaks around midday — a newsroom's working day. The UTC curve is the
same data shifted by 4–5 hours. Weekend activity runs at about half the
weekday level, which is why the causal models use **weekly** counts:
summing over a full week removes the weekly cycle by construction.

### Year-over-year seasonality

```{r yoy, eval=TRUE, fig.width=10, fig.height=4}
treated_posts |>
  count(year = factor(year(created_at)), month = month(created_at)) |>
  ggplot(aes(month, n, color = year)) +
  geom_line() + geom_point() +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:12) +
  labs(x = "Month", y = "Actions per month", color = "Year",
       title = paste("Year-over-year monthly activity:", TREATED)) +
  theme_minimal()
```

Three years of data are too few to declare "seasonality" with
confidence. What *is* unmistakable is that 2025 and 2026 sit far above
2024 in every month of the year.

## 4. An event: the November 2024 Bluesky surge

Both designs compare against the pre-event period, so first we check that
we actually have one. Without it, the `post` indicator would be all ones,
the regression would be rank-deficient, and every estimate below would be
meaningless. This exact failure hit the live collection in November 2026:

```{r event-line, eval=TRUE, fig.width=10, fig.height=4}
n_pre <- sum(treated_weekly$week < EVENT)
stopifnot("history does not reach far enough before the event" = n_pre >= 12)
c(pre_event_weeks = n_pre, post_event_weeks = nrow(treated_weekly) - n_pre)

ggplot(treated_weekly, aes(week, n)) +
  geom_line(color = "navy") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = EVENT, color = "#DC143C", linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(x = "Week", y = "Actions per week",
       title = paste("Weekly activity with event line:", TREATED)) +
  theme_minimal()
```

The break is real and it is where the story says it should be, though it
is not instantaneous. Weekly activity roughly doubles in the two weeks
after the election and keeps ramping for about seven weeks, into late
December, before leveling off around 400–450 actions a week. The
pre-event period isn't flat either: it rises through spring 2024 and
falls to a low just before the election, so the event arrives at a
seasonal trough.

## 5. Interrupted time series

ITS fits the segmented regression
*y* = β₀ + β₁·t + β₂·post + β₃·(t − t_event)·post + ε:
a pre-period trend, a level shift at the event, and a trend change after
it. The counterfactual is the pre-trend extended forward.

Read the chunk below as building the regression's design matrix by hand,
column for column as in the Python notebook:

* `t` numbers the weeks 0, 1, 2, ...;
* `post` is 0 before the event and 1 from the first post-event week on;
* `t_post` is `t − t_event` in post-event weeks and 0 before, where
  `t_event` is the index of the first post-event week, so it counts
  weeks since the event, starting at 0.

`lm()` — R's workhorse linear-regression function — then fits the model:

```{r its, eval=TRUE}
its_data <- treated_weekly |>
  mutate(
    t = row_number() - 1,
    post = as.integer(week >= EVENT),
    t_post = (t - min(t[post == 1])) * post
  )

its_fit <- lm(n ~ t + post + t_post, data = its_data)

its_table <- broom::tidy(its_fit) |>
  mutate(term = c("intercept", "trend", "level_shift", "trend_change"))
its_table

pre_mean <- mean(its_data$n[its_data$post == 0])
coefs <- setNames(its_table$estimate, its_table$term)
```

Before the election the account averaged about
**`r round(pre_mean)` actions per week**, with a pre-event trend of
`r sprintf("%+.2f", coefs[["trend"]])` per week. That trend is
statistically indistinguishable from zero: the rise through spring and
the fall into autumn roughly cancel. At the event the level jumps by
**`r sprintf("%+.0f", coefs[["level_shift"]])` actions per week**, more
than three times the pre-event average. The slope afterward changes by
only `r sprintf("%+.2f", coefs[["trend_change"]])`, so the new level
*persists* instead of decaying. That is a sustained step: a change in
the account's regime, not a passing burst of attention. (These numbers
are computed inline from the fitted model, so they always match the
table above.)

One honest caveat about the model: a single straight line is a crude
summary of a pre-period that rose and then fell. Because the event
arrives at the bottom of the autumn dip, the jump is measured from a low
point. A model of the dip, or a window starting in summer 2024, would
report a smaller level shift.

### Does R agree with Python?

Both implementations read the same archive and build the same design
matrix, so the coefficients should match the table the Python notebook
saved, up to rounding. This chunk checks:

```{r parity, eval=TRUE}
python_its <- read_csv(file.path(dirname(SHARED_ARCHIVE), "its_results.csv"),
                       show_col_types = FALSE)

parity <- tibble(term = its_table$term,
                 r = its_table$estimate,
                 python = python_its$coef) |>
  mutate(difference = r - python)
parity

if (ARCHIVE == SHARED_ARCHIVE) {
  stopifnot("R and Python ITS estimates disagree" = all(abs(parity$difference) < 1e-6))
}
```

```{r its-plot, eval=TRUE, fig.width=10, fig.height=4}
its_plot_data <- its_data |>
  mutate(
    fitted = fitted(its_fit),
    counterfactual = coefs[["intercept"]] + coefs[["trend"]] * t
  )

ggplot(its_plot_data, aes(week)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = n), color = "lightsteelblue", linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_line(aes(y = fitted), color = "navy", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_line(aes(y = counterfactual), color = "gray40", linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = EVENT, color = "#DC143C", linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(x = "Week", y = "Actions per week",
       title = paste("Interrupted time series:", TREATED),
       subtitle = "Dashed gray: pre-trend extended as counterfactual") +
  theme_minimal()
```

The gray dashed counterfactual slopes *downward*, because the pre-event
trend does. Extended far enough it would cross zero and predict negative
posts, which is impossible. A linear model of counts has no floor;
modeling log counts, or using Poisson regression (`glm(family =
poisson)`), builds one in.

### An honest aside: autocorrelation

Weekly counts are autocorrelated (this week predicts next week), which
makes OLS standard errors too small. The **Durbin–Watson statistic**
diagnoses this: values near 2 mean no first-order autocorrelation,
values well below 2 mean positive autocorrelation. The standard fix keeps
the OLS coefficients and replaces the standard errors with
**heteroskedasticity- and autocorrelation-consistent (HAC)**, or
Newey–West, errors:

```{r hac, eval=TRUE}
resids <- residuals(its_fit)
dw <- sum(diff(resids)^2) / sum(resids^2)
round(dw, 3)  # 2 = no autocorrelation; < 2 = positive autocorrelation

if (requireNamespace("sandwich", quietly = TRUE) &&
    requireNamespace("lmtest", quietly = TRUE)) {
  lmtest::coeftest(its_fit, vcov = sandwich::NeweyWest(its_fit, lag = 4, prewhite = FALSE))
} else {
  message("Install the sandwich and lmtest packages for HAC standard errors.")
}
```

With a Durbin–Watson statistic of `r round(dw, 2)`, far below 2, the
correction matters. The level shift stays clearly distinguishable from
zero, but neither the pre-event trend nor the trend change does. The
defensible claim is a *step*; the data cannot tell us whether the slope
changed.

These standard errors match the Python notebook's exactly, but only
because of `prewhite = FALSE`. sandwich's `NeweyWest()` *pre-whitens*
the residuals by default (it fits an autoregression to them first),
while statsmodels does not. HAC estimates depend on choices like this,
and on the lag length, so always report which estimator you used:
"robust standard errors" alone doesn't pin down a number.

## 6. Difference-in-differences

ITS extrapolates the treated unit's own trend; DiD instead uses a
*comparison unit* to absorb shocks common to both. Its identifying
assumption is **parallel trends**: absent the event, the two series
would have moved together. Always plot the pre-trends first:

```{r pretrends, eval=TRUE, fig.width=10, fig.height=4}
comparison_weekly <- weekly_counts(comparison_posts)

bind_rows(
  mutate(treated_weekly, account = TREATED),
  mutate(comparison_weekly, account = COMPARISON)
) |>
  ggplot(aes(week, n, color = account)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_vline(xintercept = EVENT, color = "#DC143C", linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(x = "Week", y = "Actions per week",
       title = "Pre-trend plot: treated vs. comparison account") +
  theme_minimal()
```

The DiD estimate can be computed two equivalent ways, and seeing both
demystifies the regression: first as arithmetic on the 2×2 table of
means, then as the interaction coefficient in a regression, which adds
standard errors. As in the Python notebook, the panel keeps only the
**weeks both accounts have in common**, so it is balanced:

```{r did, eval=TRUE}
# (Base R's intersect() drops the Date class, so filter with %in% instead)
common_weeks <- treated_weekly$week[treated_weekly$week %in% comparison_weekly$week]

panel <- bind_rows(
  mutate(treated_weekly, treated = 1L),
  mutate(comparison_weekly, treated = 0L)
) |>
  filter(week %in% common_weeks) |>
  mutate(post = as.integer(week >= EVENT),
         treated_post = treated * post)

means <- panel |>
  group_by(treated, post) |>
  summarise(mean_actions = mean(n), .groups = "drop")
means

did_by_hand <- with(means,
  (mean_actions[treated == 1 & post == 1] - mean_actions[treated == 1 & post == 0]) -
  (mean_actions[treated == 0 & post == 1] - mean_actions[treated == 0 & post == 0]))

did_fit <- lm(n ~ treated + post + treated_post, data = panel)
did_table <- broom::tidy(did_fit) |>
  mutate(term = c("intercept", "treated", "post", "treated_post"))
did_table
```

The `treated_post` coefficient,
**`r sprintf("%.1f", did_table$estimate[did_table$term == "treated_post"])`**,
equals the by-hand difference of differences
(`r sprintf("%.1f", did_by_hand)`). It is almost exactly the ITS level
shift, because the comparison account's own before–after change
(`post`, `r sprintf("%+.2f", did_table$estimate[did_table$term == "post"])`)
is close to zero.

### Why this DiD should not be believed

Our comparison unit is the platform's *official account*. Its posting is
driven by product launches, not by the news cycle that drives a
newsroom, and its pre-event level is more than an order of magnitude
lower. In this archive it barely moves around the event, so it subtracts
almost nothing, and the DiD collapses into a before–after comparison of
one account. A comparison too flat to absorb the shared shock (the
election news cycle) violates the design just as surely as one that was
itself treated. DiD is only as good as its comparison group.

## 7. Building a better comparison group: matching on profile covariates

A principled comparison pool: accounts similar to the treated unit on
observables. The candidates are one page of the accounts the Times
follows ([`bs_get_follows()`](https://christophertkenny.com/bskyr/reference/bs_get_follows.html)), with their profile
statistics from `bs_get_profile()`. Here is nearest-neighbor matching on (logged) followers,
posts, and account age. We log the heavy-tailed counts so one
mega-account doesn't dominate, standardize each feature with `scale()`
(subtract the mean, divide by the standard deviation, so all three are in
comparable units), and rank candidates by Euclidean distance to the
treated account. Matches are reported by rank rather than by handle:
most candidates are individual journalists, and we shouldn't rank named
people.

```{r matching, eval=bsky_authed}
candidates <- bs_get_follows(TREATED, limit = 50)

pool <- bs_get_profile(c(TREATED, head(candidates$handle, 24))) |>
  mutate(account_age_days = as.numeric(
    difftime(now("UTC"), ymd_hms(created_at, quiet = TRUE), units = "days"))) |>
  filter(!is.na(followers_count), !is.na(account_age_days))

features <- pool |>
  transmute(handle,
            log_followers = log1p(followers_count),
            log_posts = log1p(posts_count),
            account_age_days) |>
  mutate(across(-handle, \(x) as.numeric(scale(x))))

target <- features |> filter(handle == TREATED)

features |>
  filter(handle != TREATED) |>
  mutate(distance = sqrt((log_followers - target$log_followers)^2 +
                         (log_posts - target$log_posts)^2 +
                         (account_age_days - target$account_age_days)^2)) |>
  left_join(select(pool, handle, followers_count, posts_count),
            by = "handle") |>
  slice_min(distance, n = 5) |>
  transmute(match_rank = row_number(), followers_count, posts_count, distance)
```

Read the result before trusting it. Even the nearest matches have a small
fraction of the Times' audience. Matching can only choose among the
candidates you give it, and a pool drawn from the accounts a newsroom
follows contains its reporters, not its peer institutions. A better pool
would be other national news organizations, matched on covariates
measured *before* the event. See the
[MatchIt](https://kosukeimai.github.io/MatchIt/) package for the
industrial version.

## 8. Keyword volume around an event

[`bs_search_posts()`](https://christophertkenny.com/bskyr/reference/bs_search_posts.html) with `since`/`until` windows builds a topic-level
series — e.g., weekly volume of posts mentioning "twitter" around the
election. Capped to stay polite:

```{r keyword-volume, eval=bsky_authed, fig.width=10, fig.height=4}
edges <- seq(as_date("2024-10-01"), as_date("2024-12-31"), by = "week")

volume <- map2_int(head(edges, -1), tail(edges, -1), \(from, to) {
  hits <- tryCatch(
    bs_search_posts("twitter",
                    since = format(from, "%Y-%m-%dT00:00:00Z"),
                    until = format(to, "%Y-%m-%dT00:00:00Z"),
                    limit = 1000),
    error = function(e) NULL)
  Sys.sleep(0.2)
  if (is.null(hits)) NA_integer_ else nrow(hits)
})

tibble(week = tail(edges, -1), posts = volume) |>
  ggplot(aes(week, posts)) +
  geom_line(color = "navy") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = as_date("2024-11-05"),
             color = "#DC143C", linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(x = "Week", y = "Posts per week (capped at 1,000)",
       title = "Weekly volume of posts matching 'twitter'") +
  theme_minimal()
```

## 9. Saving and reloading the data

The archive and its metadata were saved when they were collected. Here we
save the *derived* tables beside this document, so the headline results
can be checked without rerunning anything. (R outputs in `RMarkdown/`
are not committed to the repository; the shared archive lives with the
Python notebook.)

```{r save, eval=TRUE}
dir.create("data", showWarnings = FALSE)

daily_both <- bind_rows(
  mutate(daily_counts(treated_posts), account = TREATED),
  mutate(daily_counts(comparison_posts), account = COMPARISON)
)

write_csv(daily_both, "data/daily_counts.csv")
write_csv(its_table, "data/its_results.csv")

reloaded <- read_csv("data/daily_counts.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
nrow(reloaded) == nrow(daily_both)
```

## 10. Research design: what it takes to claim causation

Neither design above randomizes anything. ITS assumes nothing else
changed at the event date that affects the outcome; DiD assumes parallel
trends. Both fail silently when violated. The discipline is: specify the
design *before* looking at the post-period; plot pre-trends; run placebo
tests (fake event dates, unaffected outcomes); and treat estimates as
"the effect under these assumptions," stated plainly.

Three threats loom large here. **Selection:** the treated account is on
Bluesky because a major newsroom chose to invest in the platform, a
decision that may itself have responded to the audience surge.
**Anticipation:** the weeks just before the event are a *dip*, so a
rebound from a low point would look like an effect. **Concurrent
shocks:** the election was also an enormous news event, and a newsroom
would post more after it on any platform. Natural experiments on
platforms — outages, feature launches, deplatformings — are the cleanest
events, because their timing is plausibly exogenous to any one account's
behavior.

## Ethics and limitations

Activity histories reveal sleep, work, travel, and life disruptions.
Treat even public timing data as sensitive, aggregate when reporting, and
avoid building behavioral profiles of private individuals. This document
studies two institutional accounts whose posting is professional output,
and the saved archive keeps only the account, action type, reply flag,
and timestamp. Our data are two accounts chosen for pedagogy, weekly bins
hide within-week dynamics, the author feed omits deleted posts
(survivorship in time!), and every caveat from Sections 5–7 applies to
any causal language.

## Exercises

1. Refit the ITS with daily instead of weekly counts. How do the
   estimates and their standard errors change?
2. Run a placebo ITS with a fake event date of 2024-06-01. Is the
   level shift "significant"? What does that teach you?
3. Restrict the panel to ±12 weeks around the event and refit the DiD.
4. Refit the ITS on `log1p(n)` and with `glm(family = poisson)`. Does a
   model with a floor change the story the counterfactual tells?
5. Decompose the treated series by `action` type — did original posts
   and reposts respond to the event differently?

## Research project ideas

* **Migration waves.** Using account creation dates from profiles,
  identify accounts that joined during the November 2024 surge and
  compare their retention curves to earlier cohorts.
* **Event studies of platform shocks.** Build an ITS around a Bluesky
  feature launch (e.g., DMs or video) using keyword volume as the
  outcome, with placebo dates as robustness checks.
